accroche: Chlorine reads 35.45 in every table. In 1922, Aston's spectrograph shows that no chlorine atom has that mass.
contenu_vulgarise:
Open a periodic table: chlorine carries an atomic mass of about 35.45. Then look for a chlorine atom that weighs 35.45. You won't find one: in nature, each chlorine atom weighs either 35 or 37, in atomic mass units and to a very close approximation.

## An average that chemistry could not undo

Dalton's atomic theory contained a postulate: the atoms of a given element are alike and of equal weight. In his Nobel lecture of December 12, 1922, Francis Aston recalls that the second half of that sentence was beyond the reach of chemistry. A laboratory balance weighs quantities that contain countless atoms: it gives an average, and says nothing about each atom. Aston observes that no evidence supported this postulate, and that, in his view, no theoretical doubt was nonetheless voiced publicly before the end of the 19th century.

## Weighing atoms one by one

Aston works on “positive rays”: atoms from which an electron has been torn, which an electric field accelerates and a magnetic field deflects. The deflection depends on mass. In 1912, J. J. Thomson's parabola method gives two traces for neon, one toward mass 20, the other toward 22, whereas the chemical atomic mass of neon is 20.20. Thomson at first sees in this an unknown constituent of neon.

Aston tries to separate these two neons. Thousands of distillations on charcoal cooled with liquid air yield nothing. Months of diffusion through clay finally reveal a density difference of about 0.7% between the extreme fractions. After the war, he develops the mass spectrograph, which gathers ions of the same mass onto a photographic plate: the mass can then be read off a line. For neon, the lines fall at 20 and 22, to within a thousandth, and 10% of atoms of mass 22 is enough to recover 20.20.

## The case of chlorine

Chlorine then goes through the instrument. The explanation of its fractional mass, Aston writes, was obvious from the first plate: four strong lines, at 35, 36, 37 and 38, and none at 35.46. Lines 35 and 37 are those of two kinds of atoms. Lines 36 and 38 are those of their compounds with hydrogen, hydrochloric acid. The spectrum of negatively charged particles shows only 35 and 37, and phosgene gives lines at 63 and 65, for CO³⁵Cl and CO³⁷Cl.

To recover 35.46, about one atom in four must weigh 37. The current values of the Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW) point the same way: from 75.5 to 76.1% chlorine 35, from 23.9 to 24.5% chlorine 37.

## The shift

The 35.46 of Aston's 1922 table, now 35.45 in current tables, therefore describes a mixture, not an atom. And the mixture is not exactly the same everywhere: chlorine 35 diffuses a little faster in solution, and chlorine 37 concentrates in halogen minerals. Since 2009, the CIAAW no longer gives a single value for chlorine, but an interval, from 35.446 to 35.457.

Aston draws a broader rule from this: to within a thousandth, the atoms of all measured elements have whole-number masses, with hydrogen the exception, and he himself specifies that the rule is not exact in the mathematical sense. The masses measured today, 34.9689 for chlorine 35 and 36.9659 for chlorine 37, depart from whole numbers by about three hundredths of a unit. What a table displays for an element describes a sample as much as an atom. Aston, for his part, was already counting nine isotopes for xenon.

repere.texte: On the first plate for chlorine, Aston observes lines at 35, 36, 37 and 38, and none at 35.46. Lines 35 and 37 are those of two isotopes, 36 and 38 those of their hydrochloric acids.
repere.source: Aston, “Mass spectra and isotopes,” Nobel lecture, December 12, 1922

carte.punch: No chlorine atom weighs 35.45: it is the average of two masses, 35 and 37.
carte.idee: Aston's mass spectrograph shows in 1922 lines at 35 and 37 for chlorine, and none at 35.46. The periodic-table mass is the average of a mixture: about three atoms in four of mass 35, one in four of mass 37.

quiz.question: Why does the mass spectrum of chlorine show no line at 35.46?
choix: Because Aston's apparatus distinguished only whole-number masses and rounded all the others
Because natural chlorine is a mixture of atoms of masses 35 and 37, and 35.46 is the average of the mixture
Because each chlorine atom does weigh 35.46, but ionization strips mass from it before the measurement
Because the chemical balance was weighing an impure chlorine, mixed with hydrochloric acid, which skewed the average
quiz.explication: The lines are at 35 and 37, and the natural mixture, of about three atoms of mass 35 for one of mass 37, gives 35.46 on average. The apparatus separated masses to within a thousandth, the electron torn away weighs only 0.0005 on this scale, and lines 36 and 38 are those of hydrochloric acid, not of an impurity that would skew the balance.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Aston establish that the chlorine lines at 36 and 38 are not those of isotopes?
choix: By comparing their intensity with that of the argon lines, taken as a reference
By noting that they disappear when the pressure in the tube is lowered
By observing the spectrum of negative rays, where only lines 35 and 37 remain
By measuring them on the balance after separating the fractions by distillation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On the spectrum of negatively charged rays, only lines 35 and 37 appear: lines 36 and 38 are therefore those of the compounds with hydrogen. Distillation and diffusion had achieved only a very partial separation before the spectrograph was invented.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What has the CIAAW given for the atomic weight of chlorine since 2009?
choix: A single value of 35.5, rounded for school textbooks
The value of 35.453 recommended in 1961, unchanged since
A weighted average between chlorine 35 and the rarer chlorine 36
An interval from 35.446 to 35.457, because the proportion of chlorine 37 varies slightly from sample to sample
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Since 2009 the CIAAW has given an interval, because the isotopic composition of chlorine varies from one sample to another (diffusion, halogen minerals). The 35.453 of 1961 has been replaced, and chlorine 36 exists only as radioactive traces.
